    File 1A: Literature Review Module

    Slide 1

    Literature Review Module Overview. LR Intro. Research Gap

    Slide 2

    Today: • Module and course overview; • Introduction to LR; • Research gap; • Systematic search; • Forming resarch teams.

    Slide 3

    Module and Course Overview • Graded assignments: • Literature review: 42% of the grade, team (2 people), any topic. • Research proposal: 38% of the grade, team (3 people), IT topic.

    Remember! Observe Academic Misconduct Policy. For any questions, see Course Syllabus (Moodle). Consider the research and startup opportunities available at IU.

    Slide 4

    What is a literature review?

    Slide 5

    Introduction to LR Briefly skim through paper 1 and answer the following questions: • What is the objective of the paper? • How is it structured? • How can you use this study? Briefly skim through paper 2 and answer the following questions: • What are the research questions of the paper? • What is the literature search procedure? • How is the paper structured?

    Slide 6

    Introduction to LR • A literature review is an overview of the available research for a specific scientific topic. • LR types:

    [Image Description: A diagram titled “Figure 1.1” showing three circles that represent different types of literature reviews based on their proportion within a larger text. 1. The first circle is mostly empty with a small grey shaded area at the very bottom, labeled “Background section”. 2. The second circle is half-filled with grey shading, labeled “Part of the research project write-up”. 3. The third circle is completely filled with grey shading, labeled “Stand-alone product”.]

    From SUSANNE HEMPEL Conducting Your Literature Review

    Slide 7

    The LR workflow • Select your interest: choose topic / field; • Find research gap: identify missing information; • Formulate research question or goal: define what your LR will answer; • Design search of literature: select databases & create search string; • Conduct search: search following certain critera; • Analyze & synthesize: evaluate findings.

    Slide 8

    Research Gap The starting point

    Slide 9

    Research gap exists when: • Information is missing or insufficient; • Information is biased or one-sided; • Results are contradictory; • The topic is not properly overviewed.

    Important: Research gap defines how your literature review will explore the literature. Adapted from https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK126702/

    Slide 10

    Practice Find RG Article 1 Article 2

    Slide 11

    Finding a RG •Interest: Pick a field / topic of your liking; •Gap: Search the literature for gaps in the field.

    Slide 12

    Why systematic search matters • Random search: depends on chance, not comprehensive; • Snowballing (back and forward): only sees papers citing your initial source, so - > biased, incomplete picture

    Slide 13

    Systematic Search: Choosing a Database Use databases allowing advanced search with Boolean agents: • ScienceDirect (Search Guide); • IEEE Xplore (Search Guide); • ACM Digital Library; • Dimensions AI; • OpenAlex. Avoid databases yielding no replicable search results and preprint / social media sources: • Google Scholar Search Guide; • arXiv; • ResearchGate, etc.

    Slide 14

    Building a Search String • Topic: ethics of using autonomous vehicles. • Search string template: (“main topic” OR “synonym 1” OR “synonym 2”) AND (“aspect 1” OR “aspect 2”) AND (“review” OR “literature review”) • Example of search string: (“autonomous vehicle” OR ”self-driving vehicle” OR “driverless car” OR AV) AND (ethic OR moral* OR”trolley problem*” OR “decision making” OR accountability) AND (review OR “literature review”) • Breakdown: • First group (OR): Synonyms for the main concept • Second group (OR): Ethical aspects and related terms • Third group (OR): Focus on review-type papers

    Slide 15

    Search Procedure Examples See search procedure: • Example 1; • Example 2; • Example 3. Find likely place to find inspiration for your RG: • Example 2; • Example 3.

    Slide 16

    Forming research group • Open the file provided by your instructor: use Tab 1. Forming research group; • List the topics of your liking (e.g., multiagent LLM, autonomous vehicles) in Tab 1, column B • Find someone with a similar interest and form a reseach group and put their names in column C. • Sit with the person whose interest coincides with yours and finalize the topic area you are going to explore (e.g., ethical issues of using autonomous vehicles). • Fill in Tab 2 columns B and C.

    Slide 17

    Start Searching the Research Gap • Select your database and put it in column D, • Produce a search string and put it in column D, • Example of search string: (“autonomous vehicle” OR “self-driving vehicle” OR “driverless car” OR AV OR “connected automated vehicle”) AND (ethic OR moral OR “trolley problem” OR “decision making” OR “risk distribution” OR accountability OR transparency OR “value alignment” OR “moral algorithm”) AND (review OR meta-analysis OR “literature review”) • Search for literature reviews covering your topic (use filters “review” or include “review” into your search string – see example above). • Produce a list of literature reviews covering your topic and put it in Column E. If no reviews have been found, do not register anything.

    Slide 18

    HW. Your research gap (no submission needed) • Finalize: Choose the area of your interest; • Finalize: Choose a database(s); • Finalize: Produce a search string; • Finalize: Find all literature reviews in this database relevant for your topic (use filters or keyword “review” in your search string). Register all these steps in columns C-E of the file provided by your instructor.

    Slide 19

    Today: • Have learned about the module and course overview; • Have learned more about LRs; • Have learned to identify research gaps; • Have learned about the systematic search; • Have formed reseach teams.

    File 1B: Summarizing Results & Ordering Content

    Slide 1

    Summarizing Results & Ordering Content. Critical Writing. Hedging. Citation. Tenses

    Slide 2

    Today: • Results section goals; • Ordering the citations in Results; • Critical writing; • Hedging and boosting; • Citation patterns; • Tenses in Results.

    Slide 3

    Results goal: • Cite every source selected in the search process; • Report how the sources respond to the RQ; • Provide synthesis of the sources (compare and contrast); • Report any risk of bias for any or all the sources.

    Slide 4

    Results Order 1. Distant to close: Most distantly related to your work -> Most closely related to your work; 2. Chronological: Earliest related work -> Most recent related work; 3. Comparison and contrast of different approaches or particular features or characteristics of relevant theories and research: One approach -> An alternative approach -> Another approach.

    From Weissberg R. and Buker S. Writing Up Research: Experimental Research Report Writing for Students of English

    Slide 5

    Ordering Results: Exercises • See Handout 1.

    Slide 6

    Critical Writing

    Slide 7

    Please, interpret: Brown [1] concluded that the productivity per hour increases by 5%, while several other researchers do not register any significant changes in the productivity [2], [3], [4], [5].

    Slide 8

    Interpretation available: The new SAP system for production management does not seem to yield a stable improvement in the workflow. For example, Brown [1] concluded that the productivity per hour increases by 5%, while several other researchers do not register any significant changes in the productivity [2], [3], [4], [5].

    Slide 9

    Critical Writing • Critical writing = interpretative writing; • Interpretative - > suggesting what the reader should learn about the source and how they should relate it to other sources.

    Slide 10

    Critical Writing Strategies • comparing and contrasting different theories, perspectives, concepts, and terminology from the related literature; • strategic and selective referencing to support the underpinning arguments; • arguments from two or more sources to create a new or more developed point of view; • agreeing with, confirming, or defending a finding or point of view through an analysis of its merits and limitations; • conceding that an existing point of view has some strengths but qualifying your support of the opposite position by highlighting certain weaknesses; • rejecting a point of view and giving reasons for the rejection, e.g. inadequacy, lack of evidence, and fallacies in the argument or research.

    Adapted from Hart, C. Doing a Literature Review

    Slide 11

    Approaches to Critical Writing Critical writing means presenting the sources by making inferences (conclusions) about them and referring to: • What’s known (the sources); • What’s concluded (what you infer and generalize from sources).

    Slide 12

    Critical Writing: Exercises • See Handout 2.

    Slide 13

    Revision: Hedging • Hedges (e.g., possible, might, perhaps) show uncertainty and indicate that information is presented as opinion rather than accredited fact, convey deference, modesty or respect for colleagues’ views. e.g., This idea suggests that a competition exists between nucleation at the hopper edges and within the hopper, which might account for the narrow temperature range…

    Adapted from Hyland, K. (2007). Disciplinary Discourses: Social Interactions in Academic Writing. University of Michigan Press.

    Slide 14

    Citation Patterns: Integral/Non-Integral Forms •Integral: Johnson [1], amongst other scholars, has argued that… •Non-integral: Several ways exist to address the issue of overpopulation [1].

    Slide 15

    Tenses in Results • See Handout 3.

    Slide 16

    Critical Writing: Practice • Provide a concluded inference (what you infer from sources) to unite several (at least 3) sources from your RL + synthesis (compare-and-contrast) of these sources; • Post on a Yandex Doc.

    Slide 17

    Set: TSA 5. Results Section • Submit your Results section as TSA 5 (see syllabus); • Make sure the Results are written in the Overleaf and downloaded as a PDF.

    Slide 18

    HW. Draft 1 Write-Up • Decide on the sections, if applicable; • Decide on the type of ordering (e.g., chronological); • Produce Draft 1 of your Results. Final goal: a peer reviewing team next class should be able to evaluate 1. if and why you are planning to have subsections (if applicable); 2. how you decided to order your sources; 3. the overall narrative of your future Results section.

    Today, we have learned: • What Results section aims at; • How to order citations in Results; • How to critically present the citations; • How to hedge, cite, use tenses in Results.

    Slide 4

    Visuals

    Slide 5

    Visuals - why we use them • Capture and hold reader’s attention; • Help illustrate textual information and data; • Simplify complicated textual descriptions; • Help the reader understand complicated systems, processes, and data.

    Slide 6

    [Image Description: A collage of six different types of data visualization charts. 1. Top Left - “Block diagram”: A flowchart showing the components of a system. It starts with a “Low Voltage Power Supply” which feeds into a “pH Electrode”, “Buffer Circuit”, and a “Microcontroller”. These feed into a “Summing Amplifier” and a “Reference Voltage”, ending at a “Display”. 2. Top Middle - “Scatter plot”: A graph plotting data points along an X-axis (Independent variable) and Y-axis (Dependent variable). A dotted diagonal “Trend Line” runs through the points, and one specific point far from the trend line is labeled “Outlier”. 3. Top Right - “Box plot”: A chart titled “Number of daily hospital births in Canada per day of the week”. It shows box-and-whisker plots for each day of the week (Mon-Sun) across a Y-axis ranging from 300 to 550. A caption reads “Tails of the boxplots show the min and max values.” 4. Bottom Left - “Line graph”: A graph showing changes over time. The X-axis is “time (days)” from 0 to 60. The Y-axis is “hormone (mg/ml)” from 0 to 600. It plots two lines with distinct markers: “hormone A” (circles) and “hormone D54” (triangles). 5. Bottom Middle - “Bar graph”: A 3D bar chart with an X-axis showing “condition” (A and B) and a Y-axis showing “product (mg/ml)” from 0 to 120. Condition A has a tiny bar (value 0.125), and condition B has a tall bar (value 109.14). 6. Bottom Right - “Pie chart”: A 3D pie chart divided into four segments representing geographical regions and associated numbers: US and Canada (8,898), Europe (11,139), Africa (125,657), and Asia (111,560).]

    Based on: Hoffman A., Scientific Writing and Communication, OUP, 2014

    Slide 7

    1. Photographs
    2. Block diagram
    3. Table
    4. Line graph
    5. Scatter Plot
    6. Bar graph
    7. Pie chart
    8. Box plot
    1. To present exact numerical information
    2. To show dynamic comparison, usually over time
    3. To show relationship of components of a system or a process
    4. To show actual appearance
    5. To compare data when there is no evidence of continuum
    6. To show correlation
    7. To compare parts of a whole
    8. To display differences between datasets, showing central value, variability and range

    Based on: Hoffman A., Scientific Writing and Communication, OUP, 2014

    Slide 8

    Figures guidelines: • Use figures to show trends and relationships; • Place the independent variable at the x-axis and the dependent variable at the y-axis for Graphs and Bars; • Make each figure easy to read; • Differentiate points, lines, and curves well; • Label axes and scales well; • Title should include what/where/when information. • See IEEE style guide (p.13) for the requirements of the standard. • Place the captions below the figure, format – “Fig. 1. Caption”; • Citations to figures in text always carry the abbreviation “Fig.”.

    Based on: Hoffman A., Scientific Writing and Communication, OUP, 2010 Based on: IEEE Editorial style manual for authors 2022

    Slide 9

    Example of Figure (Method)

    [Image Description: A flow diagram detailing the stages of a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) regarding Industry 4.0 in warehouse management. - “Stage 1 (Material Collection)” begins with a “Database Search: Scopus and Web of Science (WoS)” using a complex Boolean keyword string relating to Industry 4.0 and warehouse management. This yields a box stating “Total Number of Papers Obtained: 920”. - “Stage 2 (Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria)” flows through several steps: “Considering of paper that includes English as a language” (Obtained: 886) -> “Duplicate of Papers was Excluded” (Obtained: 792) -> “Inclusion of journal peer-reviewed articles” (Obtained: 136) -> “Inclusion of articles based on subjects: Scopus: Business, Management and Accounting; WoS: Business Economics, Operations Research, and Management Science” (Obtained: 97). - “Stage 3 (Finalizing the research articles)” shows the final step: “There was no room for papers if the focus was not on Industry 4.0 from the perspective of warehouse management.” leading to the final box “Total Number of Papers Obtained: 63”. Below the diagram is the caption: “Fig. 1. Summary of the steps of SLR of industry 4.0 in warehouse management was modified from (Govindan & Hasanagic, 2018; Mathiyazhagan et al., 2021).”]

    DOI: 10.1016/j.clscn.2022.100072

    Slide 10

    Example of Figure (Result)

    [Image Description: A side-by-side comparison of two images of a woman’s profile. The left image is a standard, natural-color photograph of the woman. The right image is a thermal scan of the exact same profile, displaying varying colors (blue, green, yellow, orange, red) to indicate temperature differences across her face and head. A temperature color scale bar is visible on the far right. Below the images is the caption: “Fig. 4. Digital and thermal images of a subject with simulated inflammation (hot water exposure).”]

    DOI: 10.1109/JBHI.2017.2754861

    Slide 11

    Tables guidelines • Use tables to give precise numbers or to organize data that is too detailed or complicated to be described in a text; • Place familiar context on the left and new, important information on the right; • Follow IEEE standard: • Place the caption below the table number and above the table; • Table should be numerated with Roman numerals; • Table captions should be set as an inverted pyramid; • Do not use a full stop after the caption; • See IEEE style guide (p.13) for the requirements of the standard.

    Based on: Hoffman A., Scientific Writing and Communication, OUP, 2010 Based on: IEEE Editorial style manual for authors 2022

    Examples of effective/ineffective captions Example A • Table I. Characteristics of Intestinal Flora • Table II. Soil Analysis

    Example B • Table I. Characteristics of Intestinal Flora Found for 21 Patinents with HIV-I • Table II. Soil Analysis of Six Farm Fields Near

    Based on: Hoffman A., Scientific Writing and Communication, OUP, 2010

    [Image Description: A table titled “TABLE 1 Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria”. The table has three columns: “Facet”, “Inclusion Criteria”, and “Exclusion Criteria”. - Row 1 (Scale): Inclusion is “(i) The method is practiced by at least 50 persons or six teams, working on a common product or project. (ii) The article explicitly considers itself as large-scale (either in title, abstract, or keywords).” Exclusion is “(i) The process is practiced by a single team or less than 50 persons or six teams in a large or distributed setting.     File 4B: Systematic Literature Review

    Slide 1

    Systematic Literature Review

    Slide 2

    Today: • LR Recap; • Introduction to PRISMA protocol and SLR structure; • Research Gap & Search Procedure Finalized; • RQ Drafting.

    Slide 3

    Recap: Introduction to LR • A literature review is an overview of the available research for a specific scientific topic. • LR types:

    [Image Description: A diagram titled “Figure 1.1” showing three circles that represent different types of literature reviews based on their proportion within a larger text. 1. The first circle is mostly empty with a small grey shaded area at the very bottom, labeled “Background section”. 2. The second circle is half-filled with grey shading, labeled “Part of the research project write-up”. 3. The third circle is completely filled with grey shading, labeled “Stand-alone product”.]

    From SUSANNE HEMPEL Conducting Your Literature Review

    Slide 4

    Stand-Alone LR –> Systematic LR • SLR: A review that uses explicit, systematic methods to collate and synthesise findings of studies that address a clearly formulated question* • PRISMA Protocol (see Table 1) ** • Key advantages of SLR: • Less biased: Systematic approach reduces selection bias • More comprehensive: Boolean search finds all relevant papers • Replicable: Every step documented for transparency

    *from Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions ** from PRISMA 2020 Statement

    Slide 5

    PRISMA Protocol: The SLR Standard Our Simplified Approach (Not Full PRISMA): • Define RQ/objectives clearly • Design systematic search (databases, Boolean strings) • Screen results using inclusion/exclusion criteria • Extract data from selected studies • Synthesize findings and draw conclusions

    Slide 6

    SLR structure: IMRaD model • Title • Introduction (Background + RQ + Gap) • Method (Search procedure + criteria) • Results (Search findings) • Discussion (conclusions) • References

    Slide 7

    Research Gap (Handout 1, Ex. 1) • Review the list of literature reviews found. • Identify if those literature reviews are systematic or not. • Compare and contrast these systematic literature reviews against the following parameters: • Years of research covered, • Databases used; • Features of the topic discussed. • Formulate how your future systematic literature review will be different from the existing ones (e.g., you cover different years, used a different database, discussed a different feature(s) of your topic).

    Slide 8

    Research Question and Goal What is my research about?

    Slide 9

    What is the RQ / Goal in a literature review? Ex. 1: What are the positive or negative factors influencing the intention to use SAVs [shared autonomous vehicles] (including behavioural attitude towards SAVs and willingness to use)? (Source: 10.1016/j.trf.2023.10.027) Ex. 2: This study systematically reviews the literature on the effects of using AR for patient education (e.g. information recall, perceived knowledge gain, patient satisfaction, health literacy) across all medical specialties. (Source: 10.1016/j.pec.2022.03.005) Ex. 3. In this study, a thorough systematic review of the literature on (1) trustworthy AI and AI-powered robotics, and (2) AI and AI-powered robotic applications in the AEC [architecture, engineering, and construction] is presented to prime this area of research for future studies. (Source: 10.1016/j.autcon.2022.104298)

    RQ = Goal, difference is only how you formulate it.

    Slide 10

    Your RQ/Goal Producing an effective RQ/Goal

    Slide 11

    Effective RQ/Goal • Focused on a narrow, not a broad, problem; • Would lead to new knowledge, of interest to the scholarly community; • Has not been adequately answered by the existing scholarly literature; • The researcher has a method for answering the question; • The potential answer can be tested/assessed/disputed using data/evidence; • Limited in scope (time, place, group being studied); • Researcher has the necessary skills and resources; • Project can be completed within the timescale.

    Slide 12

    Language-wise, your RQ: • clear: it provides enough specifics that one’s audience can easily understand its purpose without needing additional explanation. • focused: it is narrow enough that it can be answered thoroughly in the space the writing task allows. • complex: it is not answerable with a simple “yes” or “no,” but rather requires synthesis and analysis of ideas and sources prior to composition of an answer. • concise: it is expressed in the fewest possible words.

    Source: George Mason University Writing Center

    Slide 13

    Translating your Gap into Goal • Complete Ex. 2 in Handout 1

    Slide 14

    TSA 1. Research Gap & Objective Setting • Submit Handout 1 filled by your team as TSA 1 on Moodle. The file must incorporate the following information: • Members of team (Ivan and Mariya); • Topic (e.g., ethics of using autonomous vehicles) • Database: (e.g. ScienceDirect) • Search string (e.g., Example of search string: (“autonomous vehicle” OR “self-driving vehicle” OR “driverless car” OR AV OR “connected automated vehicle”) AND (ethic OR moral OR “trolley problem” OR “decision making” OR “risk distribution” OR accountability OR transparency OR “value alignment” OR “moral algorithm”) AND (review OR meta-analysis OR “literature review”) • (see next slide to continue)

    Slide 15

    TSA 1. Research Gap & Objective Setting • List of systematic literature reviews (if any) covering your topic; • Parameters / Features that make your future systematic literature review different from the existing ones. • Your RQ / Goal

    Slide 5

    Risk of Bias Assessment

    Bias: a process that can lead to distorted conclusions. ROB Assessment: a process that estimates how much the bias of the papers analyzed could distort the conclusions of your literature review.

    Slide 6

    Risk of Bias Assessment (Sources)

    ROB assessment process: Assessing each source for bias and reporting if any of these sources project insuffecient credibility, imperfect method design that could affect the results, small sample size or questionable population choice, intransparent/irreplicable procedure, etc. Rely on your RRE experience.

    Example: Figure 2 in Handout 1.

    Slide 7

    ROB Assessment Structure for LR

    You are supposed to provide the following assessment:

    • A table where you assess EACH source you found by stipulating what bias you detected in it, if any (see next slide);
    • A text concluding about the overall risk of bias in your LR (see the slide after the next one).

    ROB can be a separate subsection in your Results (if you have any other subsections) or a new paragraph with a table if you do not divide Results into subsections.

    Slide 8

    Example of ROB Table

    [Visual Description: A table with a black header row and alternating grey and light-grey rows below it.]

    Source Bias Description
    [1] Small sample
    [2] Non-replicable method description
    [3] No critical bias

    Slide 9

    ROB Assessment (Text)

    • ROB Assessment text, e.g.:

    • The risk-of-bias assessment reveals two studies with risk of bias. These biases are associated with insuffecient replicability of methods. One more bears no critical risks (Table I).

    Slide 10

    File 9A: Introduction to Research Proposals

    Visual Description for File 6: Standard presentation slides featuring black text on a plain white background. Slide 13 uses red text for emphasis, and slides 14 and 15 include small italicized source links at the bottom.

    Slide 1

    Introduction to Research Proposals

    Slide 2

    Today:

    • Research Proposal structure
    • Functions of the Research Proposal elements
    • Research Proposal length
    • Tenses to be used in a Research Proposal
    • Common mistakes in a Research Proposal

    Slide 3

    Research Proposal Structure

    • The Research Proposal structure can vary considerably.
    • This presentation will discuss the structure used at the Innopolis University

    Slide 4

    Research Proposal Structure

    1. Title
    2. Introduction/Background and Rationale
    3. Literature Review
    4. Methods/Methodology/Procedure/Research design
    5. Anticipated Results
    6. Discussion
    7. References

    Slide 5

    1. Title

    • Clearly summarize your research.
    • Include the keywords
    • Make it interesting.
    • Make it short (16 words max).
    • Avoid abbreviations.
    • Add a subtitle, if necessary.
    • Avoid a period in the end.

    Slide 6

    2. Introduction/Background and Rationale

    • State the problem and its significance.
    • Provide your research question(s) and/or hypothesis/-es.
    • Define the terms you use.
    • Discuss the limits you assign to your research.

    Slide 7

    3. Literature Review

    • Describe the most important theories and concepts.
    • Describe key debates and controversies for your topic.
    • Describe the research gap.
    • Make sure that your sources are relevant and credible.
    • Synthesize your sources.

    Slide 8

    4. Methodology/Procedure/Research Design

    • Briefly review the literature on the research methods.
    • Describe the methods you plan to use in your research.
    • Explain why you chose those methods.
    • Address any potential obstacles and issues.

    Slide 9

    Tips

    • Provide details of the algorithms and program logic to be used.
    • Include a timeline and budget, if necessary.

    Slide 10

    5. Anticipated Results

    • Describe the results that you think you will obtain.

    Slide 11

    6. Discussion

    • Explain the practical benefits from your research.
    • Specify if your research:
      • strengthens a theory or model;
      • challenges current theoretical assumptions;
      • creates a basis for further research.
    • Discuss potential limitations of your research.
    • Describe possible future work.

    Slide 12

    7. References

    • Follow the IEEE requirements.
    • Make sure that you have at least 15 references in total.

    Slide 13

    Research Proposal Length

    • Your text has to be four pages maximum (Visual Note: The words “four pages” are colored red and bold in the original slide)
    • References are not included.

    Slide 14

    Tenses in a Research Proposal

    • Introduction and Methods shall communicate ideas in Present Simple, Past Simple, and Present Perfect tenses.
    • Anticipated Results shall make use of Present Simple and Future Simple.
    • Discussion will mostly rely on Present Simple; however, Future Simple might be used in this section.

    Extra reference: https://www.nature.com/scitable/topicpage/effective-writing-13815989/

    Slide 15

    Common Mistakes to Avoid

    1. Submitting lengthy proposals.
    2. Covering too much research ground.
    3. Not citing major works in a literature review.
    4. Too much focus on minor issues, yet very few details on major issues.
    5. Inability to frame a persuasive and coherent argument for the proposed study.
    6. Poor grammar or careless writing.

    Source: Summary Report of Journal Operations, 2017. American Psychologist, 73 (5), 683-84. https://doi.org/10.1037/amp0000347

    Slide 16

    Important!

    • Depending on your research question, the structure of your RP can vary:
    • E.g., you can introduce Implementation as a separate section or merge it with other sections: Design and Implementation or Implementation and Results.

    Slide 17

    Practice

    • Get into groups of two.
    • Choose one of the RP samples each.
    • Fill in the Table in Handout 1 for your sample.
    • Discuss the results with your partner.
